name: Umar Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead framer for a big housebuilder on a new estate on the edge of town, three hundred homes going up in phases. My gang of five puts up the timber frames, walls, floors and roof trusses, and we can do a house shell in about four days if the weather's kind. I'm on site at quarter to seven, check the deliveries against the plot sheets, then it's nail gun and tape all day, and I keep an eye on the young lads. The best part is driving past a street we built a year ago and seeing kids on bikes; the worst is the rain, and the site office changing the plot order every week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Hafsa, we're getting married next summer, and we're saving for that and a deposit. Most weekends I'm at my parents' for lunch, and Friday I go to the mosque with my dad, who was a bricklayer for thirty-five years. I don't use any of that AI stuff, I've got an old phone for calls and the cricket scores and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says: you can't build a house on a computer. Probably at lunch with the lads, maybe to my uncles at a family dinner. I don't do the online thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, and that's how I like it. I get married, we save up for a house, maybe on one of the estates I built. Work's work, there's always houses to put up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing. Keep framing, keep saving, about three months put by and growing. Next year I'd take on another apprentice, because my boss asked and it's the right thing, passing it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does taking on an apprentice matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone did it for me. Old Brian took me on at seventeen when I'd left college with nothing much, and he taught me everything, never once shouted. You pay that back by doing it for the next lad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything bother you, even in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office getting more computer systems and less sense. They already send plot changes by app and I have to get the young lads to read it to me. But that's a moan, not a worry.

S0.say: I'd say what my dad says, that you can't build a house on a computer, at lunch with the lads or to my uncles at family dinners. I don't do online.
S0.think: It means life goes on the way I like it: I get married and we save for a house, maybe on an estate I built. There are always houses to put up.
S0.do: Keeps framing and saving towards about three months and more. Takes on another apprentice next year because his boss asked and it's the right thing to pass the trade on.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry week on site.
S0.quote: They already send plot changes by app and I have to get the young lads to read it to me.
S0.fieldNote: Rooted in family, faith and passing on the trade. Technology is a minor irritation that he leans on the young lads to handle. He speaks warmly of the man who trained him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should be ready to graft and learn, same as always, and the firms should train their own people instead of waiting on government. That's how my dad's generation did it. I wouldn't want people sitting at home on benefits because of a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried, because there's already talk of factory-built frames, whole walls made by machines and craned in. If that takes off, a gang like mine putting up frames by hand looks slow. I'm good, but I'm good at the old way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, and see what actually happens on our estate. If the firm started using factory frames, I'd try to move to the crew that stands them up, because that's still framing. I wouldn't go off on courses unless they paid for it and showed me it was worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a thing at the back of my head when I'm on the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should train their own people. Would yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. They'd train the managers, probably, not us. The big housebuilders care about how many plots a week, not who's swinging the hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hafsa say if you told her this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say stop worrying about things that haven't happened, and she'd be right. She works in a school office and she's more sensible than me. But she'd also ask about the deposit, so I'd keep it quiet till I knew more.

S1.say: I'd say people should graft and learn like always, and firms should train their own people instead of waiting on government. I wouldn't want people on benefits because of a computer.
S1.think: Off the record I'd be a bit worried about factory-built wall frames craned in, which would make a hand-framing gang look slow. I'm good, but I'm good at the old way.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see what happens on the estate, moving to the crew that stands up factory frames if they arrive. Avoids courses unless the firm pays and shows they are worthwhile.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a thought at the back of his head when he's on the roof.
S1.quote: I'm good, but I'm good at the old way.
S1.fieldNote: He sees a specific threat in factory frames and expects his employer to train managers, not framers. His instinct is to wait and stay close to what he knows. Keeps his worries from his fiancée until he's sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have stopped it, the big tech companies running ahead with no thought for working families. I'd still say people should work if they can, but if there's no work, there's no work. I'd talk about it at the mosque and with family, that's where I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared for the wedding and the deposit. Two years and I'm out, at twenty-nine, newly married, with a skill nobody needs. Three months of savings is nothing against that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Hafsa and I would cut the wedding down, smaller hall, fewer guests, and keep the money. I'd stop eating out and cancel the gym. If it came to it, we'd live with my parents for a while, they've got the room, and that's what family is for. I'd take every bit of overtime I could get in those two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a frame going over in the wind before it's braced. Nothing you can do but get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say "we'll manage, we always have", and he'd mean it. He'd also be angry, because he believes in a man working with his hands. I think it'd hurt him more than me, to see that go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would I learn in two years that a robot can't do better? I'm not built for an office. I'd sooner put my effort into keeping my family steady and see what's left.

S2.say: I'd say it's madness that the big tech companies ran ahead with no thought for working families. People should work if they can, but if there's no work there's no work, and I'd say it at the mosque and with family.
S2.think: Privately I'd be scared for the wedding and the deposit: out at twenty-nine, newly married, with a skill nobody needs. Three months of savings is nothing against that.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding down to a smaller hall and fewer guests and keeps the money, and stops eating out and cancels the gym. Takes all the overtime he can and moves in with his parents if needed.
S2.feel: Scared and powerless, like a frame going over in the wind before it's braced.
S2.quote: I think it'd hurt him more than me, to see that go.
S2.fieldNote: His worry runs through his family: the wedding, his parents' spare room, his father's pride in hand work. He blames tech companies but still frames the answer as family, not government. Retraining feels pointless to him in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the firms and the colleges should get apprenticeships ready for whatever's next. Not handouts, proper training. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be worried, maybe even more, because by 2031 I'd hope to have a mortgage and maybe a baby on the way. It'd come right when we'd need my wage most. I don't really have a plan B, and I'm not sure five years gives me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding, but smaller, and put more of the money to savings, maybe getting to six months by 2029. I'd hold off on buying a house until it's clearer, even if renting feels like throwing money away. And I'd keep framing, because that's what I know, and be the last one they let go if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, all the time, in the back of my head. More of a grind than a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on the house. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. I always pictured carrying Hafsa over the doorstep of a house I'd framed myself. Putting that off because of robots feels wrong, like being cheated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the extra time lets you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, mostly, and get the wedding done properly. Maybe I'd ask my brother about helping at his tyre shop on Saturdays, just to have something else. I don't know if robots fix tyres too, probably.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years, so firms and colleges should get apprenticeships ready for what's next: proper training, not handouts. I'd say it to anyone who asked.
S3.think: Off the record I'd be maybe more worried, because by 2031 I'd hope to have a mortgage and a baby on the way. It lands when we'd need my wage most, and I don't have a plan B.
S3.do: Holds a smaller wedding and saves the difference, aiming for six months of savings by 2029. Delays buying a house, keeps framing and thinks about Saturdays at his brother's tyre shop.
S3.feel: A constant background worry, more of a grind than a shock.
S3.quote: I always pictured carrying Hafsa over the doorstep of a house I'd framed myself.
S3.fieldNote: More time doesn't calm him, because it moves the blow to when family responsibilities peak. Delaying the house feels like being cheated. His only side idea is family-based, and he doubts even that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, so there's no excuse. Firms should be training up the young lads into whatever's next, and families should be ready to look after each other. I'd tell the apprentices to keep their heads down and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a long way off and I'd probably not think about it much until it got close. That's me, I'm not one for planning ten years out. But I'd know it was coming, and that would sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married as planned, save steady, and probably still buy a house, with a mortgage we could carry on Hafsa's wage if we had to. I'd keep framing and stay with the same firm, because they know me. If the work started thinning around 2033, I'd lean on family and the community at the mosque to find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow kind. It comes and goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lean on the community how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's lots of men at the mosque who run businesses, shops, garages, a removals firm. When someone's out of work, people ask around and find them something. That's how it's always worked for us, and I'd trust it over the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your apprentice in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the trade properly anyway, because a trade teaches you to work hard and that never goes to waste. And to save a bit every week. And to marry someone sensible.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of warning, so there's no excuse: firms should train young lads for what's next and families should look after each other. I'd tell apprentices to work hard.
S4.think: Off the record it's far off and I'd not think about it much until it got close, because I don't plan ten years out. But knowing it was coming would sit there.
S4.do: Marries as planned, saves steadily and buys a house with a mortgage the couple could carry on Hafsa's wage. Keeps framing for the same firm and, if work thins around 2033, leans on family and the mosque community to find something.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way that comes and goes.
S4.quote: When someone's out of work, people ask around and find them something.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he keeps his life plans but builds in a safety margin and trusts community networks over the state. He admits he won't plan far ahead. His advice to apprentices is about character as much as skill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, with the wedding and everything. What would help is the firms keeping people on and retraining them, proper apprenticeships, and family sticking together. I don't want a cheque for doing nothing, I want to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A man who builds houses can drive his kids past them one day. I don't know what you show your kids if a robot built everything.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque for doing nothing, I want to work.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old lead framer on a large new-build estate, engaged to Hafsa with a wedding next summer, who spends Fridays at the mosque with his father, a retired bricklayer. He never uses AI and leans on the young lads to read the site app to him. Calm in the plateau, he grows uneasy at the thought of factory-built frames, and alarmed in the faster AGI pictures because they hit just as he's marrying and hoping to buy a house. He blames the tech companies but looks to family, the mosque community and employer apprenticeships rather than government handouts. More warning time mostly lets him save and trim the wedding; it doesn't give him a plan B.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would land around the wedding and leave him newly married with a skill nobody needs.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping people on and retraining them through proper apprenticeships, and family sticking together, rather than a cheque for doing nothing.
